title: I let AI turn my personal website into an infinite runner as an easter egg
author: EngineeringFit1980
selftext:
I had a lot of fun this weekend letting Claude Code turn the background of my personal blog into a fully playable infinite runner through a forest scene, as a kind of easter egg. It even features a classic arcade-style global leaderboard.

It was a lot of fun, and my kids have been playing it for hours (it's mostly their scores on the leaderboard).

The fox model is human-made (CC0) but everything else was generated in code.

The workflow involved:

 1. Building a static 3D scene first, and getting the visuals to look nice. My plan was initially to stop there. 

 2. Then we started adding a path (initially straight, later curved), and a sphere jumping over things.

 3. Gradually I refined it, added more obstacles, brought in the fox model, and over a few more dozen iterations it turned into the game it is now.   
  
I'm quite happy with how it turned out, and tempted to start adding more biomes!

Any feedback or questions welcome. Also happy to share a link if anyone wants to play it.

comments.author: EngineeringFit1980
comments.body: One thing it failed on was when I wanted uprooted trunks to lie at an angle over the path, forcing you to go either under or over, but not through the middle. It worked okay after I explained an extrusion technique I wanted it to use, but the roots didn't look good, it struggled to line up the nodes properly. I'll probably create that model in Blender first and then put it in the game later.

comments.author: DmitryBaltin
comments.body: Looks very impressive! Could you explain how did you generate the level? Terain, road, trees...

replies.author: EngineeringFit1980
replies.body:
I started simple (simple plane for the ground, cylinders for the trees), and iteratively refined each element until it looked good to me. It's similar to how I'd build it myself, and this seems to work well for AI too. One-shot prompting doesn't usually me as good a result (sometimes you're lucky though).   
  
Also I made sure to stick to a certain palette, and added variation in the tree types, sizes and colors, and some dead trees. I didn't need to describe the trees in great detail, Claude came up with the look mostly on its own - I just said deciduous / pine / dead. I guess there are lots of examples of low poly games it could draw from.

comments.author: ThereIsNoPill6
comments.body: Cool. You should add animals coming at your from the other direction. Also you should use codex and drop claude 🙂

replies.author: EngineeringFit1980
replies.body:
Great ideas, thank you!  
  
As for Codex, to be honest, I've tried both the last couple of months. Codex is also very capable, and cheaper, and YMMV, but my subjective experience was that Codex generally filled the gaps I left in my prompts in weirder / more incorrect ways than Claude. I often had to go back and explain stuff in nitty-gritty detail to Codex where Claude would have gotten it more or less right without me explaining.

replies.author: ThereIsNoPill6
replies.body: Claude forces in their "skills" which are basically training wheels that cost a lot of tokens. Once you are pro you will hate those training wheels. When you are prompting in a generalized way claude will always appear to be better. That may be the right fit for you. No worries.
